name: php-inclusion-file-read
notes: The sink is `include $_GET['file'];` with nothing around it, which is why
this row claims a method rather than a CVE: the target demonstrates the
class, and there is no patch whose absence the verdict depends on. The
ledger's `Advisory` column says so with a dash, the way the HugeGraph and
fastjson rows do.
The control is class attribution and it is not a contrivance. Including a
file executes no command, so a results-based shell method has nothing to
compute: measured, `--methods reflected` at `--probe-depth full` sends 19
probes and reports `negative` on all 19, against the same URL the
vulnerable half confirms. That is what earns `include` its own name.
What the vulnerable half measured, 2026-10-31: 14 of 18 probes reached
`file-read`. The four that did not are depths 1 and 2 of each wrapper,
which is correct rather than a miss -- the sink runs from /var/www/html,
so a climb needs three `../` before it reaches /proc. Depth is swept for
exactly that reason: which one works is a property of the sink's own
directory, and an absolute path and a relative climb both landed here.
The expectation is `file-read` and NOT `executed`, and the reason given
here was wrong until it was measured. PHP did refuse a wrapper carrying
code in its own words -- `data:// wrapper is disabled in the server
configuration by allow_url_include=0`, php://input the same way -- and
allow_url_include has defaulted off since PHP 5.2. The conclusion drawn
from that was that the only remaining route is two-step: poison a log or
a session file, then include it. That was wrong. A script already on disk
that *writes* gets code past the setting in one step, PEAR's ships in
this image, and `php-inclusion-include-execute` reaches `executed`
against this same build.
So this case is the read half on purpose, not for want of the other, and
the two cannot share a command line: the read rungs inject into a
parameter and the write-through shape is the whole query string, so
--verify-url-location raw is required for one and fatal to the other. An
arbitrary read is a finding with its own remediation, which is why it
keeps a case and a ledger row of its own rather than being folded into
the stronger one.
The read target is /proc/version, not /etc/passwd, and that is a choice
the corpus records: proving a read needs content recognisable enough to
difference against a control, not the target's account names. /etc/passwd
is declared one safety rung up, so this default invocation never pulls it.
Both were measured against this build; only one is sent here.
